In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
carcinoma of the vagina after hysterectomy is a rare but real possibility and the risk of developing this disease is increased by a history of cervical dysplasia.
the prognosis of vaginal carcinoma following hysterectomy is related to the stage of disease and not to the indication for hysterectomy.
carcinoma of the vagina after hysterectomy for benign conditions is a rare event.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

squamous cell carcinoma of vagina following hysterectomy should be considered as a possible diagnosis in patients who present with vaginal bleeding following hysterectomy and that a thorough gynecologic evaluation is indicated.
carcinoma of the vagina is a rare but potentially fatal complication of hysterectomy.
squamous cell carcinoma of vagina following hysterectomy should be suspected when cytologic testing is positive in patients with a prior history of cervical dysplasia.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the incidence of squamous cell carcinoma in the vagina following hysterectomies for benign disease is 2.3% and that the majority of these patients will present with Stage I disease.

patients with cervical dysplasia and carcinoma in situ should be informed that there is an increased risk of vaginal neoplasia following hysterectomy and that routine follow-up with cytology is warranted for at least 10 years.
